reading.translation:
The Greeks advanced toward their opponents. The opponents fled; the Greeks pursued them, but told one another to keep their formation.

The Greeks defeated the opponents in front of them; Cyrus, however, sought his brother. The Greeks’ victory did not decide the whole battle.

Cyrus saw the king and rushed toward him. A few friends went with him. There Cyrus fell and died.

The Greeks did not see Cyrus dying. They considered the victory in their own sector great. They had not yet learned what had happened to Cyrus.

On the next day messengers came to the Greeks. They said Cyrus was dead. On hearing the report, the soldiers learned of the disaster.

The Greeks took counsel about survival. They won the struggle in their own sector, but lost Cyrus. Now they must seek a route toward Greece.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — Victory, report, and survival

blocks.title: Victory, report, and survival
body: νίκη means victory, while συμφορά means disaster. In this lesson both words describe the same battlefield at different scales. The possessive phrase ἡ τῶν Ἑλλήνων νίκη identifies whose local success is meant; it does not assert Cyrus’s accession.
ἄγγελος is a messenger and ἀγγελία a report. Follow the message from arrival to learning: ἦλθον, then ἔμαθον. These whole-event forms move the narrative through a change in knowledge.

σωτηρία, survival or deliverance, becomes the army’s new concern. βουλὴν λαμβάνειν means to take counsel: the reading uses the aorist βουλὴν ἔλαβον. Distinguish a verb’s lexical meaning from the event’s effect on the story.

sections.title: 1. Aorist indicative in past narrative
body: The indicative aorist normally locates an event in past time. An augment precedes the verbal stem, and secondary endings mark person and number. In ἔλαβον, ἐ- is the syllabic augment, λαβ- is the aorist stem, and -ον is an ending.

An aorist stem need not look like the present stem: λαμβάνω has ἔλαβον. Do not remove the augment and assume that every remaining stem is a present stem. For a vowel-initial verb the augment can instead lengthen a vowel; Lesson 22 treats that system explicitly.
The same form ἔλαβον can mean “I took” or “they took.” The noun subject or wider context resolves the ambiguity. οἱ Ἕλληνες ἔλαβον means “the Greeks took”; ἐγὼ ἔλαβον means “I took.”

checks.prompt: What marks past indicative time in ἔλαβον?
checks.answer: the augment ἐ-. The indicative aorist has augment and secondary endings.

checks.prompt: In οἱ Ἕλληνες ἔλαβον, who took?
checks.answer: the Greeks. The plural subject resolves the ambiguous -ον ending.

sections.title: 2. Thematic second aorist: active and middle
body: Thematic second aorists put ο or ε between their stem and their endings. The active pattern is ἔλαβον, ἔλαβες, ἔλαβε(ν), ἐλάβομεν, ἐλάβετε, ἔλαβον. Notice accent movement when another syllable is added.

The middle uses -όμην, -ου, -ετο, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -οντο. Compare ἐλαβόμην, “I took for myself,” with ἔλαβον, “I took.” The middle meaning depends on the verb and context; these are not the later passive aorist endings.

The infinitives are λαβεῖν (active) and λαβέσθαι (middle). Infinitives have no augment. In the teaching example ὁ στρατιώτης ἐλάβετο τὰ ὅπλα, the middle depicts the soldier taking up his own equipment.

sections.title: 3. Aspect: action viewed as a whole
body: Aspect is the way a speaker presents an action. A present stem commonly opens an action from inside, as ongoing or repeated. An aorist stem presents the action as a whole without focusing on its internal unfolding.

“Whole” does not mean “instantaneous.” οἱ στρατιῶται ἔδραμον can summarize a run that lasted some time. A duration phrase can occur with an aorist; the grammatical choice still views the event as a unit.

Keep time and aspect separate. Present φεύγουσιν means “they are fleeing” here; narrative aorist ἔφυγον means “they fled.” An aorist participle is not a past indicative: its timing is interpreted in relation to the main verb.

sections.title: 4. Active and middle aorist participles
body: The active second-aorist participle uses the stem without augment: λαβών, λαβοῦσα, λαβόν. Its masculine/neuter stem contains -οντ-; the feminine has -ουσα. Like an adjective, it agrees in case, number, and gender with the person or thing described.
The middle participle is λαβόμενος, λαβομένη, λαβόμενον and declines like an adjective in -ος, -η, -ον. Compare λαβών with λαβόμενος: both present the taking as a whole, but their voices differ.

An aorist participle often supplies an action before the main action: λαβὼν τὰ ὅπλα ἦλθεν, “having taken the arms, he came.” Context determines the relationship; the stem does not impose a separate absolute date. Accent becomes grave before a following word: λαβών → λαβὼν τὰ ὅπλα.

sections.title: 5. Common second aorists and principal parts
body: Learn the present, future, and aorist together as the first three principal parts. They identify stems needed for different systems. λαμβάνω, λήψομαι, ἔλαβον cannot be predicted by merely appending an ending to λαμβαν-.

This lesson assigns ἔρχομαι–ἐλεύσομαι–ἦλθον, φεύγω–φεύξομαι–ἔφυγον, λαμβάνω–λήψομαι–ἔλαβον, and μανθάνω–μαθήσομαι–ἔμαθον. The future middle forms may have active English meanings; their voice forms do not change the dictionary meaning automatically.

Also recognize πίπτω–πεσοῦμαι–ἔπεσον, τρέχω–δραμοῦμαι–ἔδραμον, and ἀποθνῄσκω–ἀποθανοῦμαι–ἀπέθανον in the reading. εἶπον and εἶδον receive their own focused treatment next lesson. Compounds such as ἀπέθανον are glossed now; their augment placement is taught in Lesson 24.

sections.title: Two scales of victory
body: A battle can contain successes and failures in different sectors. The Greeks drive back the troops facing them, while Cyrus’s attack brings him into direct danger near the king. The course therefore uses “Greek victory” only for the local encounter.

The expedition sought to replace Artaxerxes with Cyrus. Cyrus’s death removes that purpose even though the Greeks retain military strength. Evaluating leadership requires connecting a successful action to the aim it was meant to serve.

sections.title: Information reaches an army unevenly
body: The narrator can tell readers about Cyrus’s death before the Greek soldiers know it. This distinction matters when we judge their confidence after the battle. Their limited view of the field is part of the episode, not proof that they knew and ignored the disaster.

Messages turn that limited view into a new practical problem: survival without the expedition’s royal patron. Read the sequence of actions carefully. A reader should neither grant the soldiers the narrator’s knowledge too early nor mistake their local success for the outcome of the campaign.

sections.title: Bravery and responsibility
body: Cyrus’s personal attack can be described as bold while its consequences remain disastrous. Courage does not alone guarantee a sound decision. The reading leaves room to examine what a leader owes the many people who depend on his survival.

Compare this military aim with Cleocritus’s civic appeal in Lesson 20. One seeks a throne; the other urges citizens to recognize shared obligations after civil violence. The comparison evaluates purposes and consequences without pretending that the two speeches occurred together.
